comments.text:
Hi Shannon!

Super good points.

Re: behavior, I don't expect the sort of *in-band counseling* I show here is super effective, but the *information gathering* could be a useful input to new processes (i.e. knowing the situation could help providers decide when to step in an assist).

On pronunciation + safety precautions : well, my prompt included a pronunciation guide and lacked safety precautions, so I can credit or blame the models on those :)

author.name: Jason Davis, MD, FACR
author.headline: Founder & CEO @ iTech Clinical Intelligence | Radiology | Medicine | Computer Science | Data Science | AI

comments.text:
Josh, interesting, and thank you. I wasn’t initially a fan of GPT-Live 1 relative to GPT-Realtime, but based on your demonstration, I’ll definitely reconsider it.

We experiment with these models while developing conversational workflows for patient appointments, follow-ups, and related use cases. We’ve found that comfort with talking to computers varies by generation, particularly when the voice is perceived as artificial. Prosody and conversational timing matter.

I like the direction OpenAI is taking, and I still consider its integration of NLP and signal processing the strongest on the market. Of course, that can always change, so it’s important to remain flexible.

author.name: Benjamin Krasin
author.headline: Founder, Krasyn. Building AI for clinicians and learners, and testing it in public.

comments.text: In a medication check-in the quiet failure sits upstream of the reasoning. Benchmarking 3 speech services on our own clinical audio last week, the one we had in production dropped the "no more than" out of an acetaminophen dose limit, and another truncated a 30-second chunk of continuous speech down to 89 characters. A live model can then coordinate flawlessly over a sentence the patient never said.

comments.text: Josh Mandel, MD Whisper on Azure OpenAI was the one in production and dropped the "no more than". gpt-4o-transcribe did the truncating, and giving it the previous chunk as a prompt made recall worse, not better. Azure AI Speech fast transcription kept all 72 negated statements across 13 synthetic visits, all fed as 30-second chunks, which is not how a live voice agent hears audio.
